clips.syllabus: Virtual functions, vtable, virtual destructors
clips.title: One vtable per class, vptr set per instance
clips.hook: Where the vptr lives, how many vtables exist, and how each constructor layer sets it.
clips.summary: Each polymorphic class has exactly one static vtable, modeled as an array of function pointers. Each instance holds a vptr at offset 0 that every constructor and destructor layer reassigns to its own class's vtable.
clips.videoTitle: C++ Under the Hood: Internal Class Mechanisms - Chris Ryan - CppCon 2024

quiz.question: In a class hierarchy C : B : A with virtual functions, how many vtables exist and how many vptrs does a C object hold?
options: One vtable per class; one vptr in the object, at the same offset for all single-inheritance bases
One vtable for the whole program; one vptr per virtual function
One vtable per object; one vptr per base
One vtable per class; one vptr per data member
quiz.explanation: The vtable is per class, static. In single inheritance the object has one vptr at offset 0 shared by A, B, and C layers, which is overwritten as each constructor runs.

clips.syllabus: Object slicing, virtual calls in constructors, diamond / virtual inheritance
clips.title: Virtual calls during construction resolve to the current class
clips.hook: Trace how the vptr changes as A, B, C constructors run and why a virtual call lands in the class under construction.
clips.summary: Construction goes base-first. The vptr is set when the constructor body begins, after member initialisation, and points to that class's vtable. A virtual call from a constructor body therefore dispatches to the version for the class currently being constructed, never to a more derived override.
clips.videoTitle: C++ Under the Hood: Internal Class Mechanisms - Chris Ryan - CppCon 2024

quiz.question: Base A's constructor calls virtual foo(), and C derives from A and overrides foo. When constructing a C, which foo runs from A's constructor?
options: Undefined behavior always
A::foo, since the vptr points to A's vtable at that point
C::foo, since the dynamic type is C
It depends on whether C's members are initialised
quiz.explanation: The vptr is set to A's vtable when A's constructor body begins. C's layer has not run yet, so dispatch resolves to A::foo.

clips.syllabus: Object slicing, virtual calls in constructors, diamond / virtual inheritance
clips.title: Destruction resets the vptr outside-in
clips.hook: Why virtual calls in destructors can't reach already-destroyed derived classes.
clips.summary: Destruction runs in the reverse order of construction. Each destructor resets the vptr to its own class's vtable so virtual calls cannot reach derived overrides that touch destroyed members. Members are destroyed in reverse declaration order.
clips.videoTitle: C++ Under the Hood: Internal Class Mechanisms - Chris Ryan - CppCon 2024

quiz.question: Why does a virtual call inside ~B() dispatch to B's version rather than a derived class's override?
options: Derived classes cannot override functions called from destructors
The vptr is reset to B's vtable because derived parts are already destroyed
The compiler inlines all calls in destructors
Virtual functions are disabled for objects on the stack
quiz.explanation: By the time ~B runs, the derived part has been destroyed. The vptr is set to B's vtable so dispatch cannot reach a derived function using dead members.

clips.syllabus: Virtual functions, vtable, virtual destructors
clips.title: Pointer to virtual member function uses a thunk
clips.hook: How &Base::bar still dispatches polymorphically through a compiler-generated thunk.
clips.summary: Taking the address of a virtual member function yields a compiler-generated thunk, not the base function's address. The thunk loads the vptr, indexes the vtable slot and calls through it. A call through the pointer therefore dispatches to the override.
clips.videoTitle: C++ Under the Hood: Internal Class Mechanisms - Chris Ryan - CppCon 2024

quiz.question: What does &Foo::bar evaluate to when bar is virtual?
options: A thunk that indexes the object's vtable and dispatches
A null pointer until the object is constructed
The address of Foo::bar's code
The vtable offset only, and the call is then resolved at link time
quiz.explanation: The compiler generates a thunk that performs the vtable lookup for that slot, so the call is still polymorphic.

clips.syllabus: Virtual functions, vtable, virtual destructors
clips.title: Object layout with vptr at offset zero
clips.hook: How vptrs sit in objects under inheritance versus composition, and the virtual destructor slot.
clips.summary: With single inheritance, the vptr sits at offset 0 for base and derived alike, so a base pointer can find the vtable of any derived object. With composition, each embedded polymorphic member carries its own vptr and its own vtable assignment. A virtual destructor is placed in the vtable too.
clips.videoTitle: C++ Under the Hood: Internal Class Mechanisms - Chris Ryan - CppCon 2024

quiz.question: Why can code holding an A* find the correct vtable of a more derived C object under single inheritance?
options: The linker patches each call site
Each pointer carries a hidden type tag
The vptr is at offset 0 in both A and C
A's vtable contains every derived vtable
quiz.explanation: The vptr is at the same offset (0) throughout the chain, so the base-class view finds the most-derived vtable.

clips.syllabus: Virtual functions, vtable, virtual destructors
clips.title: Multiple inheritance: two vptrs and shared vtable
clips.hook: Why a class inheriting two polymorphic bases has two vptrs and a secondary vtable.
clips.summary: With C : A, B, the object contains an A subobject at offset 0 and a B subobject at a nonzero offset. Each subobject has its own vptr. The secondary vtable for the B part contains entries with `this` adjustment, so calls through B* reach C's overriders correctly.
clips.videoTitle: C++ Under the Hood: Internal Class Mechanisms - Chris Ryan - CppCon 2024

quiz.question: In C : A, B, why does the vtable for the B subobject need `this` adjustment entries?
options: To avoid cache misses
B's functions are always static
The vtable stores function offsets as bytes
An overrider in C expects a C* this, but a B* call passes the B subobject's address
quiz.explanation: B* points at an offset inside C, so the entry must adjust this back to the C object before running C's overrider.

clips.syllabus: Mutex implementation (futex), spinlock vs mutex, CAS/TAS, Peterson's algorithm
clips.title: Instruction Reordering Breaks Flag Sync; Fences Fix It
clips.hook: Why out-of-order execution can break flag-based sync and Peterson's, and what a memory barrier does.
clips.summary: With no data dependency between X and flag, the CPU may reorder stores in the writer or loads in the reader, so the reader can see flag=true and still read X=0. A memory barrier forbids reordering memory operations across it, which restores the ordering that Peterson's algorithm needs.
clips.videoTitle: How Hardware Makes Threads Less of a Nightmare

quiz.question: Thread 2 does X=100; flag=true. Thread 1 does while(!flag); print(X). Why might thread 1 print 0 on a modern CPU?
options: The CPU may reorder the independent stores or loads, so flag is seen set before X is
A mutex is held implicitly and blocks the write
X is stored in a register shared by both threads
The while loop is always optimized away by hardware
quiz.explanation: There is no data dependency between flag and X. Store or load reordering can make the flag update visible before X, or the load of X happen before the flag check.

clips.syllabus: Mutex implementation (futex), spinlock vs mutex, CAS/TAS, Peterson's algorithm
clips.title: Memory Models, Visibility, and the Cost of Barriers
clips.hook: Strong vs weak memory models, why visibility matters beyond reordering, and why fences are expensive.
clips.summary: Strongly ordered models make writes immediately visible to other processors, while weakly ordered models delay visibility. A barrier's core purpose is to propagate pending writes in time, and no-reordering follows from that. Barriers are costly because they restrict out-of-order execution and can disrupt other mechanisms such as branch prediction.
clips.videoTitle: How Hardware Makes Threads Less of a Nightmare

quiz.question: Why can a synchronization algorithm fail on a weakly ordered system even if no instructions are reordered?
options: Threads are always run on the same core
The cache is disabled on weak models
Weak models forbid the use of loops
Updates by one core may not yet be visible to other cores, so both threads can enter the critical section
quiz.explanation: Delayed visibility of writes across cores can let both threads see stale state and enter the critical section together.

clips.syllabus: Mutex implementation (futex), spinlock vs mutex, CAS/TAS, Peterson's algorithm
clips.title: Test-and-Set: Atomic Instruction Spinlock
clips.hook: How an atomic test-and-set instruction yields a simple spinlock with mutual exclusion.
clips.summary: Test-and-set atomically reads a boolean, sets it to true, and returns the old value. It also gives memory guarantees: pending operations complete first, and the result is visible to all cores. Spinning on it until it returns false gives mutual exclusion, and the lock is released by writing false.
clips.videoTitle: How Hardware Makes Threads Less of a Nightmare

quiz.question: Two threads execute test_and_set(&lock) simultaneously with lock=false. What happens?
options: The hardware serializes them: one gets false and enters, the other gets true and spins
Both get true and spin forever
The OS scheduler suspends both
Both get false and enter
quiz.explanation: The instruction is atomic, so executions are applied in some sequential order, and only the first sees the old value false.

clips.syllabus: Mutex implementation (futex), spinlock vs mutex, CAS/TAS, Peterson's algorithm
clips.title: Compare-and-Swap Lock
clips.hook: CAS semantics (address, expected, new, returns old) and a CAS-based lock.
clips.summary: CAS atomically compares the current value to an expected one, swaps in the new value only if they match, and always returns the original value. A lock initialized to 0 is acquired by spinning until CAS(&lock,0,1) returns 0. Release sets the lock back to 0.
clips.videoTitle: How Hardware Makes Threads Less of a Nightmare

quiz.question: In a CAS spinlock using CAS(&lock,0,1), when does a thread break out of its loop?
options: When CAS returns 1
When lock is 1 after the call
When the scheduler preempts it
When CAS returns 0, meaning it swapped lock from 0 to 1
quiz.explanation: CAS returns the original value. Returning 0 means the lock was free and this thread atomically set it to 1.

clips.syllabus: Synchronization: race conditions, mutex, semaphore, monitors, spinlocks
clips.title: Mutual Exclusion Isn't Enough: Progress and Bounded Waiting
clips.hook: Why a test-and-set lock can starve a thread, and the three critical-section requirements.
clips.summary: A TAS lock gives mutual exclusion, but one thread can keep reacquiring it and starve another. A correct solution needs mutual exclusion, progress, and bounded waiting. The bounded-waiting version uses a waiting array and hands the turn to a waiting thread in round-robin order on exit.
clips.videoTitle: How Hardware Makes Threads Less of a Nightmare

quiz.question: Which property can a simple test-and-set spinlock violate even though it ensures mutual exclusion?
options: Visibility of lock writes
Atomicity of test-and-set
Mutual exclusion
Bounded waiting
quiz.explanation: A thread that releases and immediately reacquires may win repeatedly, starving others indefinitely.

clips.subtopic: what happens when you type a URL
clips.syllabus: IP addressing, subnetting, CIDR, forwarding
clips.title: Sending a packet off-subnet: subnet check and default gateway
clips.hook: How a host decides it must hand a packet to the gateway's MAC for a 1.1.1.1 DNS query.
clips.summary: The host builds an IP packet (dst 1.1.1.1:53, random source port) over UDP, then needs a layer-2 frame. Since the destination is outside its subnet per the mask, it cannot resolve that address by ARP and instead frames the packet to the default gateway's MAC address.
clips.videoTitle: What happens when you type google.com into your browser and press enter? (Detailed Analysis)

quiz.question: A host with IP 10.0.0.2 sends a packet to 1.1.1.1. What destination IP and destination MAC go in the packet and frame?
options: Dst IP 1.1.1.1, dst MAC of 1.1.1.1 found via ARP
Dst IP 1.1.1.1, dst MAC of the gateway
Dst IP of gateway, dst MAC of gateway
Dst IP of gateway, dst MAC of 1.1.1.1
quiz.explanation: The IP destination stays the final target, while the link-layer destination is the next hop (the gateway), since the target is off-subnet.

clips.subtopic: what happens when you type a URL
clips.syllabus: NAT, reverse proxy vs forward proxy
clips.title: How NAT rewrites a DNS query and maps the reply back
clips.hook: Follow a UDP DNS query through a NAT router and see why the table entry is needed.
clips.summary: The router replaces the private source IP with its public IP, keeping or mapping the port, and records an entry in its NAT table. When the reply arrives addressed to the public IP and port, the router looks up the entry and rewrites the destination back to the private host.
clips.videoTitle: What happens when you type google.com into your browser and press enter? (Detailed Analysis)

quiz.question: Why does the NAT router keep a table entry for an outgoing DNS query?
options: To compute the checksum
To map the reply's public IP/port back to the internal host
To discover the gateway's MAC
To cache the DNS answer
quiz.explanation: The server only sees the router's public IP and port, so the router needs state to translate the reply back to the private address.

clips.syllabus: Window functions, CTEs, views, stored procedures, triggers
clips.title: Window functions: per-tuple aggregates with OVER and PARTITION BY
clips.hook: How window functions keep every row while computing aggregates, ranking, and per-partition numbering.
clips.summary: Unlike GROUP BY, a window function using OVER computes an aggregate or ranking for each tuple without collapsing rows. PARTITION BY groups tuples like a GROUP BY would, and ORDER BY inside OVER defines the ordering within each partition, enabling ROW_NUMBER and RANK.
clips.videoTitle: F2023 #02 - Modern SQL (CMU Intro to Database Systems)

quiz.question: What distinguishes a window aggregate from a GROUP BY aggregate?
options: It produces one output row per group
It only works on one table
It produces an output value for every input tuple without collapsing rows
It can't use ORDER BY
quiz.explanation: Window functions compute per-row values over a window defined by OVER, preserving all rows.

clips.syllabus: Window functions, CTEs, views, stored procedures, triggers
clips.title: RANK vs ROW_NUMBER: ties and ordering in bag semantics
clips.hook: How RANK handles ties (1,1,3), why ROW_NUMBER doesn't, and why GROUP BY can't give positions.
clips.summary: Within an ordered partition, RANK assigns equal rank to tied rows and then skips values (1,1,3), while ROW_NUMBER always gives distinct positions. Since relations are unordered bags, positional information is not available without a window function.
clips.videoTitle: F2023 #02 - Modern SQL (CMU Intro to Database Systems)

quiz.question: Two students tie for the top grade in a course and a third is next. What does RANK() OVER (PARTITION BY course ORDER BY grade) return for the third?
options: NULL
quiz.explanation: RANK gives ties the same rank and skips subsequent values, so 1,1,3.

clips.syllabus: SQL: joins (inner/outer/self), GROUP BY/HAVING, subqueries
clips.title: Nested queries: outer/inner query and column scoping
clips.hook: How to build a subquery with IN, why naive execution is slow, and how name resolution works.
clips.summary: Design the outer query first, then the inner query that supplies the predicate, linked by IN. Naive execution reruns the inner query per outer tuple, but simple cases can be rewritten as a join; column references resolve to the nearest scope.
clips.videoTitle: F2023 #02 - Modern SQL (CMU Intro to Database Systems)

quiz.question: Why is naively executing WHERE id IN (subquery) per outer tuple inefficient, and what is the usual fix?
options: It re-evaluates the inner query per tuple; the optimizer rewrites it as a join
It can't be run; use a view
It returns duplicates; fix with DISTINCT
It locks the table; fix with an index
quiz.explanation: Optimizers decorrelate or convert such subqueries into joins to avoid repeated evaluation.

clips.syllabus: Cache memory: hierarchy, locality, mapping (direct / set-associative / fully associative)
clips.title: Direct-mapped cache: address fields and conflict misses
clips.hook: How tag/set/offset bits are split and why direct-mapped lookup is fast but conflict-prone.
clips.summary: An address splits into offset (log2 B bits), set (log2 M/B bits) and tag (the rest). Lookup checks a single line, but blocks mapping to the same set evict each other even when the cache has free space.
clips.videoTitle: 14. Caching and Cache-Efficient Algorithms

quiz.question: A direct-mapped cache has size M, line size B, and w-bit addresses. How many tag bits are stored per line?
options: w - log2(B)
w - log2(M) - log2(B)
w - log2(M/B)
w - log2(M/B) - log2(B)
quiz.explanation: Offset takes log2 B bits and set index log2(M/B) bits, so the tag is w - log2(M/B) - log2 B = w - log2 M.

clips.syllabus: Cache memory: hierarchy, locality, mapping (direct / set-associative / fully associative)
clips.title: Set-associative caches: k-way sets and bit fields
clips.hook: Hybrid between direct-mapped and fully associative: how set count and tag bits change with k.
clips.summary: With k ways, there are M/(kB) sets, so the set field has log2(M/kB) bits and only k lines in the set are searched. k=1 gives a direct-mapped cache and k=M/B gives a fully associative cache. Eviction happens within the block's own set.
clips.videoTitle: 14. Caching and Cache-Efficient Algorithms

quiz.question: A 32 KB cache with 64 B lines is 4-way set-associative. How many set-index bits does an address use?

clips.syllabus: Cache write policies (write-through/back), replacement, miss types (3 Cs)
clips.title: Cold, capacity and conflict misses
clips.hook: Distinguish the 3 Cs by asking what a fully associative cache would have done.
clips.summary: Cold misses are first accesses. Capacity misses occur because the working set exceeds the cache even if it were fully associative. Conflict misses occur because too many blocks map to one set and would not have been evicted under full associativity.
clips.videoTitle: 14. Caching and Cache-Efficient Algorithms

quiz.question: A 16-way set-associative cache repeatedly cycles through 17 blocks of the same set while most of the cache is empty. This miss is a:
options: Cold miss
Conflict miss
Sharing miss
Capacity miss
quiz.explanation: A fully associative cache could hold all 17 blocks, so the evictions come from set mapping, which makes them conflict misses.

clips.syllabus: Cache write policies (write-through/back), replacement, miss types (3 Cs)
clips.title: Why a 32x32 submatrix column thrashes a 4-way cache
clips.hook: Work out the address arithmetic that maps a whole column of a submatrix into one cache set.
clips.summary: With 4096-double rows, consecutive column elements differ by 2^15 bytes. This changes only the tag bits, so all accesses land in the same set of a 4-way cache and evict one another, causing conflict misses.
clips.videoTitle: 14. Caching and Cache-Efficient Algorithms

quiz.question: Rows are 2^15 bytes apart, with 6 offset bits and 7 set bits. Why do column accesses map to the same set?
options: Stride 2^15 only changes bits above the set index (the tag)
The offset bits change each row
The cache is too small to hold the matrix
Row-major order forces same-set mapping
quiz.explanation: Adding multiples of 2^15 leaves the low 13 bits (offset and set) unchanged, so only the tag differs.

clips.syllabus: Cache write policies (write-through/back), replacement, miss types (3 Cs)
clips.title: Fixing conflict misses: padding and copying
clips.hook: Break power-of-two strides by padding rows or copying tiles into temporary buffers.
clips.summary: Padding rows by a small constant changes the set index across rows and spreads accesses over sets. Alternatively, copy the submatrix into a small temporary. For cubic-work matrix multiply the quadratic copy cost is a lower-order term.
clips.videoTitle: 14. Caching and Cache-Efficient Algorithms

quiz.question: Why does padding each row of a power-of-two-width matrix reduce conflict misses?
options: It increases the line size
It reduces cold misses
It increases cache associativity
It makes the stride vary the set-index bits instead of only the tag
quiz.explanation: A non-power-of-two stride changes the set and offset bits, so column elements spread across sets.

clips.syllabus: Cache write policies (write-through/back), replacement, miss types (3 Cs)
clips.title: LRU vs optimal replacement: the 2M/2Q lemma
clips.hook: LRU on a cache twice as large incurs at most twice the misses of an optimal policy.
clips.summary: Sleator–Tarjan: if an algorithm incurs Q misses on an ideal cache of size M, then LRU on a fully associative cache of size 2M incurs at most 2Q. For asymptotic analysis, one can therefore assume optimal replacement or LRU interchangeably.
clips.videoTitle: 14. Caching and Cache-Efficient Algorithms

quiz.question: An algorithm incurs Q misses on an ideal cache of size M. What does the LRU lemma guarantee?
options: LRU on a size-M cache incurs exactly Q misses
LRU on a direct-mapped cache of size 2M incurs at most 2Q misses
LRU on a fully associative cache of size 2M incurs at most 2Q misses
LRU on size M incurs at most Q/2 misses
quiz.explanation: The lemma states that with double the cache size, LRU is within a factor of 2 of optimal replacement.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Sink Parameters: Take by Value, Then std::move
clips.hook: Why a by-value parameter plus std::move beats const& for constructors, and when it backfires.
clips.summary: A const& parameter forces a copy into the member because const objects cannot be moved. Taking the argument by value and moving it into the member costs one move for rvalues and one copy for lvalues, but it is only a win when moves are cheap, as with std::string and unlike an array of a million doubles.
clips.videoTitle: Nicolai Josuttis - Let's Move - Meeting C++ 2020

quiz.question: Why can a constructor `Email(std::string v) : value(std::move(v))` outperform `Email(const std::string& v) : value(v)` for rvalue arguments, and when does the trade-off turn bad?
options: The by-value version avoids the copy for rvalues by moving; it is bad when the type's move is expensive (e.g. a member that is a large std::array)
The by-value version never allocates; it is bad when the string is long
The compiler converts it into a const& automatically; it is bad only in debug builds
Moving from a const& is allowed so both are identical; by-value is bad only for ints
quiz.explanation: A const& argument cannot be moved from, so the member is always copy-constructed. By value, an rvalue argument is moved into the parameter and then into the member. This helps only if moves are cheap, and for types like std::array<double,N> a move is a full copy.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Ref-Qualified Overloads: Safe and Fast Getters
clips.hook: Overload a member function on the value category of *this to return by value only for temporaries.
clips.summary: Returning a const reference to a member is fast but dangling if the object is a temporary, as in a range-based for over `next().getValue()`. Overloading getValue on `&&` (return by value) and on `const&` (return reference) gives a safe result for dying temporaries and no copies for named objects.
clips.videoTitle: Nicolai Josuttis - Let's Move - Meeting C++ 2020

quiz.question: Why overload `getValue() &&` to return by value and `getValue() const&` to return a reference?
options: The && overload binds to temporaries that may die, so a by-value return avoids dangling, while named objects keep the cheap reference
It lets the compiler skip the destructor of the temporary
It forces RVO to apply to the member
The && overload is called for const objects, so it must copy
quiz.explanation: Overload resolution prefers the && overload for rvalue objects (temporaries). Returning by value there avoids a dangling reference when the temporary is destroyed. For lvalue objects the object outlives the call, so the reference return is safe and fast.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Moved-From Objects: What remove_if Does to Your Invariants
clips.hook: A defaulted move copies the enum state but moves the string, leaving an Email that claims to be valid with no value.
clips.summary: Algorithms such as remove_if move elements internally, so moved-from objects are ordinary objects that may get touched again, including by the destructor. A memberwise move leaves the string empty while the trivially-copied enum still says valid, breaking the class invariant, so moved-from objects should stay in a consistent state.
clips.videoTitle: Nicolai Josuttis - Let's Move - Meeting C++ 2020

quiz.question: Why does a default memberwise move of a class with a std::string and an enum state field leave a moved-from object that breaks an invariant?
options: The string is copied while the enum is moved
The move constructor is deleted so the object is destroyed
The enum is set to zero by move
The string is moved and becomes empty, but the enum is just copied and still says 'valid'
quiz.explanation: Moving a std::string leaves it valid but typically empty, while moving a scalar enum is just a copy. The two members become inconsistent, so an object claiming validity has an empty value.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: Disabling Moves: Why =delete Is Wrong and Rule of Five Nuance
clips.hook: Deleted move operations suppress the copy fallback; defaulting the copy operations is the way to disable moves.
clips.summary: A deleted move constructor still takes part in overload resolution and is chosen, so rvalues fail to compile instead of falling back to copy. Declaring the copy operations as default disables moving. This shows the Rule of Five means 'think about the others', not 'declare all five'.
clips.videoTitle: Nicolai Josuttis - Let's Move - Meeting C++ 2020

quiz.question: How should you disable move semantics for a class while keeping it copyable?
options: Declare move constructor and assignment as =delete
Declare move operations private
Declare the copy operations (e.g. =default) and do not declare move operations
Mark move operations noexcept(false)
quiz.explanation: A deleted move is found by overload resolution and causes an error for rvalues. If the move operations are not declared, rvalues bind to the const& copy operations. Declaring a copy operation suppresses the implicit move operations, so defaulting the copies disables moves.

clips.syllabus: Move semantics, rvalue references, Rule of 0/3/5
clips.title: noexcept Move Operations and vector Reallocation
clips.hook: Why std::vector copies instead of moves on growth unless your move constructor is noexcept.
clips.summary: push_back's strong exception guarantee means the vector cannot move elements during reallocation if a move might throw, because it cannot roll back. Marking move operations noexcept lets reallocation use moves, and a defaulted move gets noexcept deduced automatically.
clips.videoTitle: Nicolai Josuttis - Let's Move - Meeting C++ 2020

quiz.question: Why does std::vector::push_back use a move constructor during reallocation only if it is noexcept?
options: Throwing moves can't be called on heap memory
noexcept moves are faster at the instruction level
The standard forbids throwing moves
A throwing move would leave already moved elements unrestorable, violating the strong guarantee
quiz.explanation: If a move throws partway through, the source elements are already modified and cannot be rolled back. The vector therefore falls back to copying unless the move is noexcept, as with std::move_if_noexcept.

clips.syllabus: Perfect forwarding, universal references, emplace_back vs push_back
clips.title: Universal References: Binding Both const and Temporary Containers
clips.hook: Why `const T&` loses constness info and `T&` rejects temporaries, and how T&& deduction solves both.
clips.summary: A non-const lvalue reference cannot bind to a temporary, while a const reference makes everything const. A T&& parameter in a deduced context binds to lvalues and rvalues and keeps their constness. std::forward is unnecessary when the argument is only used, not passed on.
clips.videoTitle: Nicolai Josuttis - Let's Move - Meeting C++ 2020

quiz.question: Why does a function template `void print(T&& coll)` accept both a const vector lvalue and a temporary vector, while `print(T& coll)` rejects a temporary?
options: T&& always means an rvalue reference to a temporary
T&& copies the argument into a local
T&& is a forwarding reference: T deduces as an lvalue-reference type for lvalues and a plain type for rvalues; T& cannot bind to rvalues
T& adds const automatically and so can't bind
quiz.explanation: For deduced T, T&& is a forwarding reference. Lvalues deduce T as X& (with reference collapsing) and rvalues deduce T as X, so both bind with constness preserved. A non-const T& cannot bind to rvalues.

clips.syllabus: Copy elision, RVO/NRVO
clips.title: Why std::move on a Member Return Is Not Blocked by RVO
clips.hook: Copy elision applies only to local objects, not to members of the object the function is called on.
clips.summary: Returning a member from an rvalue-qualified getter creates no local object, so RVO and NRVO cannot apply. Returning std::move(member) by value is therefore the right way to avoid a copy.
clips.videoTitle: Nicolai Josuttis - Let's Move - Meeting C++ 2020
